Abstractive Text Summarization with a Transformer Built from Scratch

DSL 504 Natural Language Processing: Group Assignment 2, Question 3

Group members: ⟦PENDING: names and roll numbers⟧

Abstract

We implement the Transformer encoder-decoder of Vaswani et al. (2017) from basic PyTorch layers and train it to write multi-sentence summaries of news articles from the CNN / Daily Mail dataset. The attention, feed-forward, positional-encoding, encoder-layer and decoder-layer code is our own; only the tokenizer is pre-trained. The model has 15.2 million parameters (d_model 256, 4 heads, 4 encoder and 4 decoder layers) and is trained on all 287,113 training pairs with teacher forcing, the paper's warm-up learning-rate schedule and early stopping on the validation loss. Summaries are generated with greedy decoding and scored with ROUGE on the full test set of 11,490 articles. A first run with the paper's exact learning rate stalled (validation loss 4.51, ROUGE-1 13.65); with half the learning rate and twice the batch size, the final model reaches a validation loss of 2.32 and ROUGE-1 36.72, ROUGE-2 15.32, ROUGE-L 25.67 and ROUGE-Lsum 34.33. This is 3.3, 2.2 and 2.0 points below the Lead-3 baseline on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-Lsum, and 0.65 points above it on ROUGE-L. The model has learned to copy from the article through attention, and its cross-attention forms clear alignments between summary and article words. Its main weaknesses are repetition and phrases that are copied correctly but attached to the wrong person or thing.

Key facts at a glance

Item Value
Tokenizer Pre-trained bert-base-uncased WordPiece, 30,522 sub-words + 1 added [NL] token = 30,523, shared by articles and summaries
Truncation Articles: first 512 tokens. Summaries: first 127 tokens, plus a start or end token (128 decoder positions)
Model d_model 256, 4 heads (d_k 64), 4 encoder + 4 decoder layers, d_ff 1024, dropout 0.1, tied embeddings
Parameters 15,186,688
Training-set size 287,113 pairs (the full training split)
Training runs Run 1: the paper's learning-rate schedule, batch 32 (stalled). Run 2: half the learning rate, batch 64 (32 x 2 accumulation steps). The final model is chosen by validation loss: run 2, epoch 20 (validation loss 2.324, perplexity 10.2)
Decoding Greedy, at most 128 tokens, no teacher forcing
ROUGE on the test set (F1, 11,490 articles) ROUGE-1 36.72 / ROUGE-2 15.32 / ROUGE-L 25.67 / ROUGE-Lsum 34.33 (Lead-3: 40.06 / 17.48 / 25.02 / 36.36; Table 7)

1. Introduction

Abstractive summarisation means writing a summary in new words, rather than copying sentences out of the article (extractive summarisation). It is a sequence-to-sequence problem: the input is a news article of several hundred words and the output is a short summary of three or four sentences.

We use the Transformer encoder-decoder from "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017). The encoder reads the whole article and builds a contextual representation of every token. The decoder writes the summary one token at a time; at every step it looks back at the summary written so far (masked self-attention) and at the article (encoder-decoder attention). We implement every component ourselves, train the model on CNN / Daily Mail, evaluate it with ROUGE, compare it with the Lead-3 baseline, study its outputs and visualise where it attends while it writes.

2. Dataset and preprocessing

2.1 Dataset

We use CNN / Daily Mail version 3.0.0 (Hermann et al., 2015; Nallapati et al., 2016). Each example is a news article and its "highlights", three or four sentences written by the journalists, separated by newline characters. The highlights are the reference summaries.

Table 1. Dataset splits and how we use them.

Split Pairs Used for
Training 287,113 Training the model (all of it)
Validation 13,368 Validation loss after every epoch, early stopping, choosing the checkpoint
Test 11,490 Final ROUGE scores only, never for training or tuning

The dataset is loaded with load_dataset("abisee/cnn_dailymail", "3.0.0"). This is the same dataset as the assignment's load_dataset("cnn_dailymail", "3.0.0"); recent versions of the Hugging Face hub only accept the namespaced name. No split contains an empty article or summary, so no example was dropped and the test set is complete.

2.2 Preprocessing pipeline

Preprocessing is done once by prepare_data.py (using data.py), and the result is cached as NumPy arrays.

  1. Lowercasing and whitespace. All text is lowercased and every run of whitespace is collapsed to a single space. Lowercasing matches the uncased tokenizer.
  2. Sentence separator. The \n between highlight sentences is replaced by a special [NL] token. The BERT tokenizer treats a newline as ordinary whitespace, so without this the sentence boundaries would be lost. ROUGE-Lsum needs them: it compares the summaries sentence by sentence, with sentences separated by \n in both the reference and the output. The model learns to produce [NL] between sentences, and when token ids are turned back into text every [NL] becomes \n again.
  3. Sub-word tokenization. We use the pre-trained bert-base-uncased WordPiece tokenizer (Devlin et al., 2019), which the assignment allows. Its vocabulary of 30,522 sub-words is extended with [NL] (id 30,522), giving 30,523 entries. Articles and summaries share this one vocabulary. Sub-words mean there are no out-of-vocabulary words: a rare word or name is split into known pieces, for example "123rd" becomes 123 ##rd.
  4. Truncation. Each article is cut to its first 512 tokens and each summary to its first 127 tokens (Section 2.3).
  5. Start and end tokens. Every summary gets the start token [CLS] (id 101) in front and the end token [SEP] (id 102) at the end. We reuse these existing special tokens instead of adding new ones.
  6. Padding. Sequences are padded with [PAD] (id 0) to a fixed length (512 for articles, 129 for summaries) and stored as uint16 arrays. When a batch is built, the columns that are padding in every row of the batch are removed, so all sequences in a batch have the same length but no compute is wasted on padding beyond the longest sequence in the batch.

Decoder input and target. The summary [CLS] w1 ... wn [SEP] gives the decoder input (shifted right, starts with the start token) and the prediction target (shifted left, ends with the end token). Table 2 shows this for the first test example, whose summary has 40 tokens including the start and end tokens.

Table 2. Decoder input and target for test example 0.

Position 1 2 3 4 ... 17 18 ... 39
Decoder input [CLS] membership gives the ... . [NL] ... last word
Target membership gives the icc ... [NL] israel ... [SEP]

The article of the same example begins ( cnn ) the palestinian authority officially became the 123 ##rd member of the international criminal court on wednesday , ....

2.3 Length statistics and the truncation limits

Table 3. Length in WordPiece tokens after lowercasing (summary lengths include the [NL] tokens).

Split Article median Article 90th pct Article max Articles > 512 Summary median Summary 90th pct Summaries > 127
Train 798 1,479 6,321 79.8% 61 97 2.7%
Validation 763 1,474 2,415 75.7% 67 109 4.4%
Test 778 1,502 2,965 76.6% 64 102 3.4%

Figure 1. Article and summary lengths in the training split, with the truncation limits.

The assignment's table was measured on 2,000 test articles. On the first 2,000 test articles we get an article median of 639 tokens, a 90th percentile of 1,301, a maximum of 2,965, 62% longer than 512 tokens, and a summary median of 49 (47 without [NL]). The assignment reports 641, 1,304, 2,967, 62.5% and 49, so our tokenization matches. The full test split has longer articles (median 778) than this sample, so Table 3 gives the statistics of every full split.

Why 512 article tokens. About 77-80% of the articles are longer than 512 tokens, so most are truncated. This loses little, because news articles put the key facts first (the "inverted pyramid" style). We measured it on the test set: 86.3% of the distinct words of a reference summary appear somewhere in the full article, and 80.8% already appear in its first 512 tokens. So the truncated article still contains about 94% of the reference words that the article contains at all. 512 tokens keep a median of 437 words per article. A longer limit would also be expensive: self-attention cost grows with the square of the length, and 512 is the upper end of the range the assignment suggests.

Why 127 summary tokens. Only 2.7% of the training summaries are longer than 127 tokens, so almost every summary is kept whole. With the start or end token this gives 128 decoder positions, which matches the maximum generation length.

3. Model architecture

All model code is in model.py. It uses only nn.Linear, nn.Embedding, nn.LayerNorm, nn.Dropout and plain tensor operations. No nn.Transformer, nn.TransformerEncoder(Layer), nn.TransformerDecoder(Layer), nn.MultiheadAttention, F.scaled_dot_product_attention, Hugging Face model class or pre-trained weight is used.

3.1 Overview

article ids (B, S)
  -> Embedding x sqrt(d_model) + positional encoding -> dropout
  -> 4 x EncoderLayer [ self-attention -> feed-forward ]
  -> memory (B, S, 256) ------------------------------------------+
                                                                  |
summary shifted right (B, T)                                      |
  -> Embedding x sqrt(d_model) + positional encoding -> dropout   |
  -> 4 x DecoderLayer [ masked self-attention                     |
                        -> encoder-decoder attention  <-----------+
                        -> feed-forward ]
  -> Linear (weights tied to the embedding) -> logits (B, T, 30,523)

B is the batch size, S the article length and T the summary length. The encoder and decoder share one embedding table, because articles and summaries share one vocabulary.

3.2 Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention

The core formula is

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) + mask ) V

MultiHeadAttention projects the queries, keys and values with three nn.Linear(256, 256) layers, splits each into 4 heads of size d_k = 64, applies the formula to every head in parallel, concatenates the heads and applies an output projection nn.Linear(256, 256). The central lines:

q = self._split_heads(self.w_q(query))                  # (B, H, Tq, Dk)
k = self._split_heads(self.w_k(key_value))              # (B, H, Tk, Dk)
v = self._split_heads(self.w_v(key_value))
scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(self.d_k)  # (B, H, Tq, Tk)
scores = scores.masked_fill(~mask, torch.finfo(scores.dtype).min)
weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)                 # each row sums to 1
out = self.attn_dropout(weights) @ v                    # (B, H, Tq, Dk)
out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, Tq, H * Dk)
return self.w_o(out), weights

Masking replaces a blocked score with the most negative finite number, which after the softmax gives a weight of exactly zero, the same as adding minus infinity. A finite value is used so that a row in which every position is blocked would give a uniform row instead of NaN. The same module serves as self-attention (query and key_value are the same sequence) and as encoder-decoder attention (the query comes from the decoder, key_value is the encoder output). It also returns the attention weights, which we use for the visualisation in Section 7.

3.3 Position-wise feed-forward network

FFN(x) = max(0, x W1 + b1) W2 + b2

Two linear layers, 256 -> 1024 -> 256, with a ReLU in between (and dropout after the ReLU), applied to every position separately.

3.4 Positional encoding

Attention by itself ignores word order, so a fixed sinusoidal encoding is added to the token embeddings:

PE(pos, 2i)   = sin( pos / 10000^(2i / d_model) )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i / d_model) )

The table is computed once for 512 positions and stored as a buffer, so it is not trained. As in the paper, the embeddings are multiplied by sqrt(d_model) = 16 before the encoding is added, and dropout is applied to the sum.

3.5 Encoder and decoder layers

Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Dropout(Sublayer(x))), the post-norm form of the original paper.

  • Encoder layer: multi-head self-attention, then the feed-forward network.
  • Decoder layer: masked multi-head self-attention over the summary so far, then encoder-decoder attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder output), then the feed-forward network.

The model stacks 4 encoder layers and 4 decoder layers. Dropout (0.1) is applied to the embeddings, to every sub-layer output, to the attention weights and inside the feed-forward network.

3.6 The three masks

Masks are boolean tensors in which True means "may attend".

Table 4. Masks.

Mask Shape Used in Blocks
Source padding mask (B, 1, 1, S) Encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention Padding tokens of the article
Causal (look-ahead) mask (1, 1, T, T) Decoder self-attention Later summary positions
Target padding mask (B, 1, 1, T) Decoder self-attention (combined with the causal mask by AND) Padding tokens of the summary

The causal mask is lower-triangular: position t may attend to positions 1 to t only. For T = 4:

1 0 0 0
1 1 0 0
1 1 1 0
1 1 1 1

3.7 Output layer and initialisation

A final linear layer maps each decoder output vector to 30,523 vocabulary logits. Its weight matrix is shared with the embedding table (weight tying; Press and Wolf, 2017, also used in the Transformer paper), which saves 7.8 million parameters. Weight matrices are initialised with Xavier-uniform initialisation. The embedding table is initialised from a normal distribution with standard deviation d_model^-0.5, so that after scaling by sqrt(d_model) the embeddings have roughly unit variance, and the row of the padding token is set to zero.

3.8 Configuration and parameter count

Table 5. Model configuration, compared with the paper's base model.

Hyperparameter Ours Transformer base (paper)
d_model 256 512
Attention heads (d_k) 4 (64) 8 (64)
Encoder / decoder layers 4 / 4 6 / 6
Feed-forward size d_ff 1,024 2,048
Dropout 0.1 0.1
Vocabulary 30,523 (shared) 37,000 (shared BPE)
Parameters 15,186,688 about 65 million

Parameter breakdown:

Part Parameters
Shared embedding / output projection (30,523 x 256) 7,813,888 (51.5%)
Encoder: 4 layers x 789,760 (attention 263,168 + feed-forward 525,568 + 2 LayerNorms 1,024) 3,159,040
Decoder: 4 layers x 1,053,440 (2 attentions 526,336 + feed-forward 525,568 + 3 LayerNorms 1,536) 4,213,760
Total 15,186,688

Half of the parameters are in the embedding table, which is typical for a small model with a large vocabulary. The configuration is within the range the assignment suggests (d_model 256-512, 3-6 layers per stack, 4-8 heads) and fits comfortably on an 8 GB GPU.

3.9 Greedy decoding

At test time there is no teacher forcing. greedy_decode encodes the article once and reuses the encoder output at every step. It starts from [CLS], runs the decoder on the tokens generated so far, takes the most probable next token, appends it and repeats, until every summary in the batch has produced [SEP] or 128 tokens have been generated. The padding and start tokens are never chosen, and a sequence that has finished just receives padding while the rest of the batch continues. With return_attention=True, the function also records the encoder-decoder attention of the last decoder layer at every step, which is what Section 7 visualises. For simplicity the decoder is re-run on the whole prefix at every step (no key/value cache); this is slower but gives the same result.

3.10 Checking the implementation

sanity_checks.py tests the implementation before any real training:

Check Result
The model contains no built-in Transformer or attention modules Passed
Causal mask: changing a later summary token never changes the output at earlier positions Passed
Padding masks: adding padding to the article or the summary does not change the outputs Passed
Attention weights sum to 1 and padding positions get zero attention Passed
Copy task: a small model is trained to copy random sequences, then greedy decoding must reproduce them 96% copied exactly (loss 0.005)

The copy task exercises the whole pipeline end to end (embeddings, positional encoding, both attention types, the masks, training and greedy decoding). A model with a broken causal mask or broken cross-attention cannot pass it. The first two checks test directly for common pitfalls 2 and 3 of the assignment.

4. Training

4.1 Setup

Table 6. Training configuration.

Setting Value
Training data All 287,113 training pairs, reshuffled every epoch
Loss Cross-entropy over the vocabulary, padding positions ignored (ignore_index = 0)
Teacher forcing Decoder input = gold summary shifted right; the whole summary is trained in one parallel pass
Optimiser Adam, beta = (0.9, 0.98), eps = 1e-9
Learning-rate schedule lr = factor x d_model^-0.5 x min(step^-0.5, step x warmup^-1.5), warm-up 4,000 steps; factor 1.0 in run 1 (the paper's schedule, peak 9.88e-4) and 0.5 in run 2 (peak 4.94e-4)
Batch size Run 1: 32 articles (8,972 optimizer steps per epoch). Run 2: 64 articles, as 2 accumulated batches of 32 (4,486 steps per epoch)
Gradient clipping Global norm 1.0
Precision bf16 mixed precision (the loss is computed in fp32)
Validation Loss on all 13,368 validation pairs after every epoch
Early stopping Stop after 3 epochs without improvement; at most 20 epochs
Checkpoint for testing The best validation-loss checkpoint (best.pt), never the last one
Seed 42
Hardware NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU (8 GB), PyTorch 2.14.1 + CUDA 13.0
Speed About 12,000-13,000 target tokens per second, about 26 minutes per epoch including validation (run 2: 522 minutes for 20 epochs)

Teacher forcing. During training the decoder input is the gold summary shifted right, so the model predicts every summary token in one parallel pass. The causal mask makes sure that position t only sees the gold tokens before it, so the model cannot copy the answer.

Loss. The cross-entropy is averaged over the real target tokens only; padding positions are ignored in both the training and the validation loss (common pitfall 4). The validation loss is the average over all non-padding target tokens of the validation split.

Learning-rate schedule. The learning rate rises linearly for the first 4,000 optimizer steps and then decays in proportion to 1/sqrt(step). With the paper's schedule (run 1) the peak is 9.88e-4, falling to 6.6e-4 at the end of epoch 1 and 4.7e-4 at the end of epoch 2. Run 2 multiplies the schedule by 0.5 (peak 4.94e-4). Because run 2 accumulates two batches per optimizer step, its warm-up lasts almost a whole epoch. The warm-up keeps the early updates small while Adam's statistics are still unreliable, which matters for post-norm Transformers.

Figure 2. The learning-rate schedules of the two training runs, plotted against epochs.

Early stopping. After every epoch the model is evaluated on the validation split. When the validation loss improves, the model is saved as best.pt. Training stops after 3 epochs in a row without improvement, and the evaluation script always loads best.pt (common pitfall 7).

4.2 Two training runs

We trained the model twice. The assignment allows the validation split to be used for choosing hyperparameters, and every decision below is based on the validation split only.

Run 1: the paper's schedule, batch 32 (runs/base).

Epoch Training loss (epoch mean) Validation loss Validation perplexity
1 5.416 4.566 96.1
2 4.650 4.510 90.9 (best)
3 4.591 4.592 98.7

The training loss stopped falling at about 4.6 after roughly 10,000 steps (1.1 epochs) and stayed there for the next 1.5 epochs, and the validation loss rose in epoch 3. A 15-million-parameter model trained on 287,113 articles should keep improving for much longer, so we examined the epoch-2 checkpoint on validation articles:

  • It uses the article only weakly. On 128 validation pairs, its loss is 4.58 with the correct article and 5.15 when each summary is paired with a different article. So the article tells the model the topic, but little more.
  • Its cross-attention is almost uniform. On 5 validation articles, the entropy of the last decoder layer's cross-attention is 94% of the entropy of a uniform distribution, and the largest attention weight is on average only 1.5 times the uniform weight (1/512). The decoder averages the whole article instead of looking at particular words.
  • The encoder has not collapsed. The mean cosine similarity between the encoder's output vectors at different positions is about 0.7, so the positions are still distinguishable; the decoder simply has not learned to use them.
  • The summaries are generic and repetitive, for example "the doctor is now in a hospital" repeated three times for an article about a kidney donation chain.

In short, run 1 learned a topic-conditioned language model of summaries: it writes fluent-looking text about the right subject but cannot copy names, numbers or facts from the article. We attribute this to a learning rate that is too high for our batch size. The paper's schedule was designed for batches of about 25,000 tokens, while our batches of 32 summaries contain only about 2,000 target tokens, so the gradient is much noisier. With noisy, large updates, a post-norm Transformer can get stuck on the easy solution (predicting likely summary words from the topic) and never learn the sharp encoder-decoder alignments needed for copying.

Because the validation loss had risen and the training loss had been flat for 1.5 epochs, we stopped run 1 by hand after epoch 3 instead of waiting two more epochs for early stopping, and kept its best checkpoint (epoch 2) as a fallback.

Run 2: half the learning rate, batch 64 (runs/lr05_b64). We changed only two settings: the learning-rate factor from 1.0 to 0.5, and the batch size from 32 to 64 (two accumulated batches of 32, because of GPU memory). Everything else, including the model, the data and the seed, is the same.

Run 2 trained for the full 20 epochs (89,720 optimizer steps, 8.7 hours). Early stopping never triggered: the validation loss did not improve in epochs 18 and 19 (2 of the 3 allowed epochs) but reached its lowest value in epoch 20.

Epoch Training loss (epoch mean) Validation loss Validation perplexity
1 5.934 4.441 84.9
2 4.330 3.837 46.4
3 3.931 3.495 32.9
4 3.596 3.096 22.1
5 3.298 2.831 17.0
6 3.081 2.686 14.7
7 2.944 2.599 13.4
8 2.849 2.552 12.8
9 2.778 2.508 12.3
10 2.722 2.472 11.8
11 2.678 2.459 11.7
12 2.641 2.438 11.5
13 2.609 2.408 11.1
14 2.581 2.386 10.9
15 2.557 2.385 10.9

19 2.483 2.362 10.6 (no improvement, 2/3)
20 2.469 2.324 10.2 (best)

Run 2 behaves very differently. Already after one epoch its validation loss (4.441) was below the best of run 1, and its cross-attention had become focused: the entropy fell to 64% of uniform and the largest weight rose to 62 times the uniform weight. Its outputs started to contain names and details from the article ("swansea striker ...", for an article about a Swansea player). In epoch 2 the validation loss dropped sharply from 4.44 to 3.84, which is when the model learned to copy from the article. After that it kept falling, more and more slowly, until the end of training (Section 5.1).

The validation loss is lower than the training loss in every epoch. This is expected: the training loss is averaged over the whole epoch while the model is still improving, and dropout is active only during training.

Model selection. Run 2's best validation loss (2.324, perplexity 10.2, epoch 20) is far below run 1's best (4.510, perplexity 90.9), so run 2's best checkpoint is our final model. The choice was made on validation loss alone; the test set was used only to report the final scores of both runs. Because run 2's validation loss improved in the last epoch, its best checkpoint and its last checkpoint happen to be the same epoch. The evaluation still loads best.pt (common pitfall 7).

5. Quantitative results

5.1 Loss curves

Figure 3. Validation loss (solid) and mean training loss (dashed) per epoch for both runs.

Figure 4. Run 2 (the final model): training loss every 100 optimizer steps (light line) and per epoch (dots), validation loss after every epoch, and the best checkpoint (dashed line), which is the one used for testing.

Figure 5. Run 1: the training loss levels off at about 4.6 after roughly 10,000 steps and the validation loss rises in epoch 3.

Run 2's validation loss falls quickly for the first five epochs (from 4.44 to 2.83) and then more and more slowly: by about 0.04 per epoch around epoch 10, and by 0.00 to 0.03 per epoch after epoch 13. Two small rises (epochs 18 and 19) are followed by the best value, 2.324, in epoch 20. The training loss keeps falling as well (2.47 in epoch 20), and the gap between training and validation loss stays small and does not grow, so there is no sign of overfitting. The model was still improving slightly when the 20-epoch limit ended training, so more epochs would probably lower the loss a little further, but with clearly diminishing returns. The light per-step training curve in Figure 4 drops a little at the start of every epoch, when the model sees the same articles again. This is a mild sign of memorisation of the training set, but it does not stop the validation loss from improving.

5.2 ROUGE on the test set

All scores are F1 x 100 on the full test set (11,490 articles), computed with the rouge_score package with stemming (use_stemmer=True). The generated token ids are converted back to text before scoring, and the references are the original highlights. ROUGE-L treats each summary as a single sequence and finds the longest common subsequence. ROUGE-Lsum splits both summaries into sentences at \n and computes the longest common subsequence sentence by sentence; it is the standard variant for CNN / Daily Mail. The two give very different numbers, so we report both.

Table 7. ROUGE F1 on the CNN / Daily Mail test set.

System ROUGE-1 ROUGE-2 ROUGE-L ROUGE-Lsum

Lead-3 (our ROUGE setup) 40.06 17.48 25.02 36.36
Run 1 (best = epoch 2, greedy) 13.65 1.62 10.97 12.62
Run 2, final model (best = epoch 20, greedy) 36.72 15.32 25.67 34.33

Our Lead-3 scores (first three sentences of each article, split with NLTK's sentence tokenizer) reproduce the assignment's numbers exactly, which confirms that our ROUGE setup is the standard one.

System ROUGE-1 P / R / F1 ROUGE-2 P / R / F1 ROUGE-L P / R / F1 ROUGE-Lsum P / R / F1

Lead-3 has much higher recall than precision because its three article sentences are much longer than the reference highlights (78.7 words on average, against 52.9; Table 9). Run 2's summaries are about as long as the references (56.1 words), so its precision and recall are balanced. Its precision is higher than Lead-3's on every ROUGE type (for example ROUGE-1 36.6 against 34.4), but its recall is much lower (39.3 against 52.4).

Numbers written as words in the article ("three") count as present when the summary writes the digit. evaluate.py splits on whitespace instead and reports 55.0, 67.1 and 58.7 words per summary for the references, run 1 and run 2.

Run 1 almost always repeats itself: 99.9% of its summaries contain a repeated three-word sequence and 44.5% contain a whole sentence twice. 99.4% of its 4-grams do not occur in the article and 13.6% of its summaries contain a number that is not in the article, which confirms that it writes generic text instead of using the article.

Run 2 fixes most of these problems. Only 0.6% of its summaries contain a number that is not in the article (8.3% of the references do, because the journalists add facts), its length distribution is close to the references', and only one summary reached the 128-token limit. Two problems remain:

  • Repetition. 64.8% of its summaries repeat a word trigram, nine times the rate of the references, and 11.7% contain a whole sentence twice. Repetition costs less ROUGE than it seems: deleting the repeated sentences (a diagnostic only; the reported scores are unchanged) would raise ROUGE-1 from 36.72 to 37.09 and ROUGE-Lsum from 34.33 to 34.72, less than half a point.
  • It is much more extractive than the references. Only 1.4% of its words and 39.3% of its 4-grams are absent from the article, against 11.9% and 80.0% for the references, and 22% of its sentences are copied word for word (3.9% for the references). The model has learned mainly to select, cut and join article phrases, not to rephrase.

Like the references, run 2 takes much of its content from the start of the article: 44.7% of its copied 4-grams first occur in the Lead-3 sentences, against 40.7% for the references.

5.4 The gap to Lead-3

The final model is 3.34 ROUGE-1, 2.16 ROUGE-2 and 2.03 ROUGE-Lsum points below Lead-3 and 0.65 ROUGE-L points above it. Table 10 compares the two article by article. The 95% intervals come from a paired bootstrap over the 11,490 articles (2,000 resamples), and none of them contains zero, so every difference is larger than the sampling noise.

Table 10. Run 2 compared with Lead-3, article by article (F1 x 100).

ROUGE-1 ROUGE-2 ROUGE-L ROUGE-Lsum
Mean difference, run 2 minus Lead-3 -3.34 -2.16 +0.65 -2.03
95% bootstrap interval -3.55 to -3.12 -2.36 to -1.96 +0.46 to +0.85 -2.24 to -1.81
Articles on which run 2 scores higher 37.0% 39.9% 53.6% 41.8%

The ROUGE-L advantage comes from precision (25.5 against 21.4), not from recall (27.5 against 32.9). Plain ROUGE-L finds a single longest common subsequence over the whole summary, so Lead-3's long output is penalised, while run 2's summaries are about as long as the references. On ROUGE-Lsum, the standard measure for this dataset, Lead-3 is still 2 points better. Run 2 scores higher than Lead-3 on 37-42% of the articles, so it is competitive on many of them but not on average.

For context, See et al. (2017) report ROUGE-1/2/L of 36.44 / 15.66 / 33.42 for their pointer-generator network and 39.53 / 17.28 / 36.38 with coverage, against 40.34 / 17.70 / 36.57 for their Lead-3. They used the original Perl ROUGE script, whose ROUGE-L on newline-separated sentences corresponds to our ROUGE-Lsum, and beam search, so the comparison is only rough. Still, our greedy 15-million-parameter model without a copy mechanism lands in the same range as the pointer-generator network without coverage.

The reasons for the remaining gap, as far as our results show them:

  1. Lead-3 is a very strong baseline on CNN / Daily Mail. News is written in the inverted-pyramid style, and the highlights often restate the first sentences. Even dedicated neural models of the time did not beat it (see above). Our model mostly copies article phrases (Table 9), so it competes with Lead-3 on Lead-3's own ground. Lead-3 copies whole, correct sentences, while our model cuts and joins phrases and sometimes joins them wrongly (Section 6.3).
  2. Content selection. Repetition costs less than half a point (Section 5.3), so most of the gap comes from choosing the wrong content, or from repeating a fact instead of adding a new one. Lead-3's recall is 13 ROUGE-1 points higher than ours.
  3. No pre-training. Our model learns English, facts about the world and summarisation from 287,113 articles alone. Models that beat Lead-3 clearly, such as BART (Lewis et al., 2020; ROUGE-1 44.16), are pre-trained on far more text and have hundreds of millions of parameters.
  4. No copy mechanism. The model learned to copy through attention alone (Section 7), and it copies multi-piece names correctly. Producing every copied token from the output vocabulary still leaves room for errors such as "1680" for the article's "1728" (Section 6.2). Pointer-generator networks add an explicit copy distribution for this.
  5. Model size and compute. 15 million parameters and 8.7 hours on one laptop GPU, compared with 65 million parameters for the base Transformer. The validation loss was still falling slowly at the 20-epoch limit.
  6. Greedy decoding and exposure bias. The model is trained on gold prefixes but generates from its own predictions. A wrong token cannot be undone, and greedy decoding tends to repeat phrases (64.8% of the summaries). Beam search with trigram blocking usually adds ROUGE points.
  7. Truncation. About 6% of the reference words that occur in an article fall beyond the first 512 tokens (Section 2.3), a small loss.

6. Qualitative analysis

6.1 How the examples were chosen

qualitative.py selects the examples automatically from the test predictions so that they are not cherry-picked: three random articles, the article with the median ROUGE-1 (a typical output), the best and the worst article by ROUGE-1, the two summaries with the most repeated word trigrams, and two summaries that contain a number not found in the article. For every example it lists the start of the article, the reference and the generated summary, and three automatic flags: repeated trigrams, numbers not in the article and words not in the article. We checked every flag against the article by hand before calling something an error.

6.2 Examples

Six test articles generated by the final model (run 2) follow, taken from runs/lr05_b64/eval_test/qualitative_examples.md. Two were random samples, one is the median article, and three are failure cases. Generated text is shown as the model produces it: lowercased, with WordPiece's spaces around punctuation. Scores are F1 x 100 for that article.

Example 1: test #6311, random sample (ROUGE-1 43.9, ROUGE-2 20.0, ROUGE-Lsum 40.9). A correct summary built by copying.

  • Article (start): "A new HIV treatment pioneered using an antibody to attack the virus could lead to a new vaccine to prevent the infection. The first results to emerge from patient trials reveal the experimental therapy can dramatically reduce the level of virus in a patient's blood - their viral load. ..."
  • Reference: New antibody blocks protein receptor needed to infect human cells. / Patients injected saw 300-fold reduction in amount of HIV in their blood. / Scientists believe breakthrough could result in new vaccines against virus.
  • Generated: the first results to emerge from patient trials reveal the experimental therapy can dramatically reduce the level of virus in a patient ' s blood - their viral load. / the antibody was designed by researchers to block the key viral protein receptor that is needed to infect human blood cells. / as a result patients injected with the neutralising antibody during the trials saw a 300 - fold reduction in their viral load. / the scientists believe the therapy could pave the way for an hiv vaccine after clinical trials revealed the treatment resulted in a 300 - fold decrease in the amount of hiv.
  • Comment: Every statement is correct and the three facts of the reference are all present. The first three sentences are article sentences 2, 4 and 5 copied word for word. The fourth is article sentence 6 shortened: "Scientists at the Rockefeller University in New York believe a new antibody therapy ..." becomes "the scientists believe the therapy ...". This is extraction plus compression, not paraphrase. The 300-fold reduction is stated twice.

Example 2: test #6890, random sample (ROUGE-1 56.2, ROUGE-2 31.9, ROUGE-Lsum 51.2). Good content, repeated last sentence.

  • Article (start): "Loneliness is often associated with elderly people ... But a new report released today reveals that it is in fact younger people who feel more lonely than older generations ... The survey, funded by the Big Lottery, found that more than 80 per cent of young people feel lonely at some point. ... Chloe Jackson, 19, appeared on today's This Morning to talk about how Facebook makes her feel lonely."
  • Reference: Younger people feeling lonelier than older generations according to report. / 43% of 18 to 34-year-old wish they had more friends. / Many only interact with friends online. / Chloe Jackson, 19, said Facebook makes her feel lonely. / Feels left out when she sees friends' posts when they're out having fun.
  • Generated: survey found more than 80 % of young people feel lonely at some point. / 43 % of 18 to 34 - year - olds admitted they wished they had more friends. / many admitted they were more likely to interact with friends online than face - to - face. / chloe said facebook often made her feel like she was left out of fun. / she said facebook often made her feel like she was left out of fun.
  • Comment: The first four sentences are correct and cover most of the reference: the 43% figure, meeting friends online and Chloe feeling left out. "Per cent" is rewritten as "%". The last sentence repeats the fourth with only the subject changed ("chloe" -> "she"). The model has no memory of what it has already said, so after a sentence boundary the same continuation is again the most probable.

Example 3: test #2652, median ROUGE-1, a typical output (ROUGE-1 36.5, ROUGE-2 14.5, ROUGE-Lsum 34.9). A wrong description of a person.

  • Article (excerpts): "Nathan Hughes on Friday night had his ban for accidentally knocking out George North sensationally over-turned on appeal ... The Wasps No 8 was initially suspended for three matches ... Captain James Haskell said: 'Astounded would be an under-statement' ... Hughes was sent off and then banned for three weeks following the incident on March 27."
  • Reference: Nathan Hughes accidentally knocked out George North during Northampton's 52-30 victory against Wasps on March 27. / The Wasps No 8 was initially suspended for three matches. / Hughes missed his side's Champions Cup defeat against Toulon. / It was North's third blow to the head in the space of two months. / The Welsh winger has been advised to take a month off from playing.
  • Generated: nathan hughes missed his side ' s champions cup quarter - final loss against toulon last sunday. / the fiji - born forward missed his side ' s champions cup quarter - final loss against toulon last sunday. / the saints captain was sent off and banned for three weeks following the incident. / the ban was thrown out as the appeal lodged by wasps was up - held.
  • Comment: Sentences 1 and 4 are correct. Sentence 2 repeats sentence 1 with a different name for the same person ("the fiji-born forward", adapted from the article's "the Fiji-born player"). Sentence 3 copies the ban correctly but calls Hughes "the saints captain". He plays for Wasps, the Saints (Northampton) were the opposing team, and the captains named in the article are Wasps' James Haskell and Harlequins' Joe Marler. "Saints" does not occur in the article at all; the model brought it in from the training data, where Northampton are often called the Saints. The key fact that this was North's third head injury is missing.

Example 4: test #10377, repeated phrases (ROUGE-1 39.4, ROUGE-2 16.9, ROUGE-Lsum 36.5). Repetition and a fact attached to the wrong person.

  • Article (excerpts): "Missoula: Rape and The Justice System in a College Town, a Doubleday publication that was released Tuesday ... Krakauer, the author of the critically acclaimed book Into the Wild, sat down for an interview with ABC's Nightline ... Brave: Kelsey Belnap (left) and Allison Huguet (right) were among the five women profiled ... Miss Belnap allegedly had been gang-raped by four college football ..."
  • Reference (first 3 of 7 sentences): Author of 'Into the Wild' spoke to five rape victims in Missoula, Montana. / 'Missoula: Rape and the Justice System In a College Town' was released April
  • / Three of five victims profiled in the book sat down with ABC's Nightline Wednesday night. / ...
  • Generated: missoula : rape and the justice system in a college town doubleday publication that was released tuesday. / missoula : rape and the justice system in a college town, a doubleday publication that was released tuesday. / (the same sentence a third time) / miss belnap, the author of the critically acclaimed book into the wild, sat down for an interview with abc ' s nightline. / (the same sentence again)
  • Comment: The book title sentence appears three times and the last sentence twice. The last sentence is fluent and every word is in the article, but it is false. It joins the subject "Miss Belnap" (one of the women in the book) to the predicate of a different sentence about the author, Jon Krakauer. Checks for words or numbers that are not in the article cannot catch this kind of error.

Example 5: test #178, number not in the article (ROUGE-1 34.7, ROUGE-2 8.2, ROUGE-Lsum 32.0). A wrong number.

  • Article (excerpt): "New research indicates that "Double Falsehood," a play first published in 1728 by Lewis Theobald, was actually written more than a century earlier by Shakespeare himself ... "Double Falsehood," also known as "The Distressed Lovers," is based on the "Cardenio" section of Don Quixote ..."
  • Reference: New research indicates that a play published in 1728 was written by William Shakespeare. / Scholar Lewis Theobald had passed the work off as his own. / Texas researchers used software to analyze and compare the language of the men.
  • Generated: shakespeare ' s " double falsehood " play first published in 1680 by lewis theobald. / shakespeare ' s " double falsehood " was written more than a century earlier by shakespeare himself. / the play is based on the " cardenio " section of don quixote.
  • Comment: The year is wrong: the article says 1728, and 1680 occurs nowhere in it. The model copied the sentence structure but generated the year from its vocabulary, where a plausible but wrong number won. Sentences 2 and 3 are correct (the Cardenio detail is in the article). The software analysis by the Texas researchers, a key point of the reference, is missing.

Example 6: test #184, lowest ROUGE-1 (all scores 0). A contradiction and the wrong focus.

  • Article (start): "Over the last year more than 25,000 people, a population about the size of Key West, Florida, have fought Ebola infections. More than 10,000 have not survived. But for those who have survived, life will never be the same. ..." Later: "In Liberia and Sierra Leone, the number of cases has fallen so much, there are more treatment facilities than demand."
  • Reference: April 8, 2014, the WHO finally started reporting the Ebola epidemic was a "concern" / Front line health care workers and Ebola survivors say the world has to act quicker.
  • Generated: more than 25, 000 people have survived, but many have survived. / there are more treatment facilities than demand. / there are more treatment facilities than demand.
  • Comment: The first sentence contradicts the article: 25,000 people were infected, and more than 10,000 of them died. The model joined "more than 25,000 people" with "have survived" from the following sentences. The second sentence is copied correctly but loses its context (it applies only to Liberia and Sierra Leone) and is then repeated. The article is an opinion piece whose main point, that the world reacted too slowly, is not in its first sentences, and the model misses it.

The highest-scoring summary (ROUGE 100, test #1036) is again a CNN Student News page. The model writes the boilerplate highlights for all 4 such test articles, and 3 of them score ROUGE 100 (run 1 managed 2 of the 4). This is a memorised template that occurs 322 times in the training summaries, not summarisation.

6.3 Failure analysis of the final model

To estimate how often the final model makes factual errors, we read nine summaries against their full articles. These are the summaries that were not chosen because they failed: the three random samples, the median article and the five attention examples of Section 7 (test articles 0 to 4).

  • Correct and covers the main points: 2 of 9 (#6311, #6890, the latter with a repeated sentence).
  • Correct but misses the main event: 2 of 9. Test #4 never says that a noose was hung at Duke University; it starts with "student was identified during investigation by campus police". Test #3 says that five Americans "are monitored" and omits that they have been released.
  • Garbled quotations: 1 of 9 (#663). Film reviews are copied without saying who wrote them, and one is cut and repeated: "delivers that with direct visceral rush of an epipen rush of an epipen".
  • At least one clear factual error: 4 of 9 (#2652, test #0, #1, #2), always of the same kind (see below).

Nine summaries are too few for a precise rate, but the pattern is consistent. Table 11 groups the failure types, with automatic counts over the whole test set where a count is possible.

Table 11. Failure types of the final model.

Failure type How often (11,490 test summaries) Examples
Repeated phrases and sentences 64.8% repeat a word trigram (references 7.2%); 11.7% contain a whole sentence twice. Many more repeat a fact in other words #10377, #6890, #2652, #184; test #0: "officially officially officially officially"
Copied phrase attached to the wrong subject (wrong name or wrong role) Not countable automatically; 4 of the 9 summaries read in full #10377 (Belnap as the author of Into the Wild), #2652 ("the saints captain"), test #0 ("the united states says it is a state party to the rome statute", said of Palestine; the US opposed it), test #1 (a dog "found dead after being hit by a car in january", which the article says of a cat), test #2 (Section 7.2)
Wrong number 0.6% contain a number that is not in the article (references 8.3%); a correct number in the wrong place is not counted #178 (1680 for 1728), #184 (25,000 "have survived")
Words or facts not in the article 29.2% contain a word of 4+ letters that is not in the article (references 94.6%), mostly harmless changes such as "says" for "said" #2652 ("saints"), test #2 ("for the past month")
Misses the main point Not countable; 2 of the 9 #184 (ROUGE 0), test #3, test #4
Copies instead of rewriting 22% of the generated sentences are copied word for word (references 3.9%) #6311
Habits from the training data 193 summaries (1.7%) start with "new :", as 9,827 training highlights (3.4%) do ("NEW:" marks updated CNN stories), but no test highlight does. The CNN Student News template is reproduced for all 4 such articles test #0, #213; #1036
Too short or too long Rare: 1.8% under 30 words, 1.4% over 100 words, 1 summary hit the 128-token limit none

The most important error is the wrong-subject error. Each part of the sentence is copied correctly, often from neighbouring sentences, but the parts are joined so that a fact is attributed to the wrong person, country or animal. These sentences are fluent and use only article words, so they look trustworthy, and checks for words or numbers that are not in the article cannot find them. They come from the decoding process: the decoder chooses each token from the current prefix and its attention over the article. When a name is followed by a predicate that is likely in that context (the author of, sent off, a state party), attention jumps to the place in the article where that predicate occurs, whoever its subject was there (Section 7.2 shows this in a heatmap). Compared with run 1, the model has moved from inventing text to recombining article text, so its errors are now errors of composition rather than invention.

6.4 Failure modes of run 1

The stalled first run shows in an extreme form what happens when the decoder does not use the article. All examples below are from runs/base/eval_test/qualitative_examples.md.

  1. Degenerate loops. For an article about a new HIV antibody therapy (test #6311) the summary starts "dr. dr. dr. dr. dr. paul mc mc mckinkinkinkink..." and repeats the WordPiece ##kin until the sentence ends. Once greedy decoding produces a token whose most likely successor is itself, it cannot escape.
  2. Generic text about the right topic. For a review of the film "Furious 7" (test #663) it writes "the film was filmed on the show in the film ' s film ' the film '" three times. For an article about ISIS beheadings (test #717, the median example) it writes "the group is the most popular in the world". The topic word is right; nothing else is.
  3. Invented facts, names and numbers. For an article about the Moors murderer Ian Brady (test #11079) it writes "dr. paul mckinnon, 44, was found dead in his home in the early hours of sunday morning". The person, the age and the event are all invented. For an article about a basketball player taking a girl with Down syndrome to the prom (test #5) it writes "the former nfl star ... at the age of 14"; the number 14 does not occur in the article.
  4. Unrelated text. For an article about Anne Frank's date of death (test #12) it produces "new : the new : the family is " not a " hero "", with no word in common with the reference (all ROUGE scores 0).
  5. Memorised templates. Its single perfect summary (ROUGE 100, test #492) is a CNN Student News page. These pages all share the same boilerplate highlights ("This page includes the show Transcript ..."), and 322 training summaries are this template, so the model has memorised it. This is memorisation, not summarisation.

7. Attention visualisation

7.1 Method

visualize_attention.py generates a summary for one test article with greedy decoding and records the encoder-decoder (cross) attention of the last decoder layer at every generation step, that is, while the model writes the summary by itself, not during teacher-forced training. Row t of the heatmap is the attention the model paid to the article when it generated token t. The main figure averages the 4 heads; a second figure shows each head separately. Rows are the generated summary tokens and columns are article tokens, with the tokens as axis labels. A whole 512-token article is unreadable, so the plot shows the 60-token window of the article that receives the most attention, and the title states what share of the attention falls inside this window.

7.2 Final model (run 2)

We show test example 2, an article about the Iranian foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif. It is the same article as run 1's heatmap in Figure 8, so the two can be compared directly. For this figure we drew all 66 generated tokens instead of the default 40, so that the third sentence is included (--max_rows 70 --window 70).

Figure 6. Final model (run 2), test example 2: cross-attention of the last decoder layer, mean of the 4 heads, recorded during greedy generation. Rows are the 66 generated tokens, and the columns are article tokens 22-91, which receive 37% of the attention. The generated summary is "mohammad javad zarif is a u.s. secretary of state john kerry's opposite number. / zarif has been u.s. secretary of state john kerry's opposite number in securing nuclear talks. / zarif has been a u.s. secretary of state for the past month." The article begins "... certain things you doubtless know about Mohammad Javad Zarif. He is, of course, the Iranian foreign minister. He has been U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry's opposite number in securing a breakthrough in nuclear discussions ...".

What the heatmap shows.

  • Copying is a diagonal. While the model writes "mohammad java ##d za ##ri ##f", each WordPiece attends to the same piece in the article, with weights up to 0.42, about 200 times the uniform weight of 1/512. The same happens for "u . s . secretary of state john kerry ' s opposite number". The decoder copies by looking at the article token it is about to write and then moving one position to the right. Run 1 had to produce names from the vocabulary without such alignment and wrote "ahmadinejad" instead (Figure 8).
  • Compression is a jump. After "zarif", the attention jumps over ". he is, of course, the iranian foreign minister. he has been" straight to "u . s"; the words "is a" have weak, spread-out attention. This is how the model shortens sentences.
  • Paraphrase is visible too. When writing "nuclear talks", the model attends to "nuclear" and "discussions": it writes a synonym while looking at the original word.
  • Function words and punctuation ("is", "a", ".", [NL]) get diffuse attention. The decoder predicts these from its own context, not by copying.
  • Sharp attention does not mean a correct output. In the third sentence the model attends to "u . s . secretary of state" just as sharply as in the first two, but stops before "john kerry ' s opposite number". The result, "zarif has been a u.s. secretary of state", is false: he is Iran's foreign minister. This is the wrong-subject error of Section 6.3 as it happens: a correctly copied span after the wrong subject. The rows for "for the past month" are diffuse, with no clear source in the article, and the phrase is indeed invented.
  • Repetition is visible as returning to the same span. The decoder copies the span "u . s . secretary of state" three times, once in every sentence. Nothing in the model records which article tokens it has already used. A coverage mechanism (See et al., 2017) adds exactly this record, to stop repetition.

Figure 7. The same example, each of the 4 heads of the last decoder layer separately.

All four heads show the same copy diagonal, with small differences in sharpness. On the five attention examples (test articles 0 to 4), the heads' average normalised entropy is between 0.72 and 0.75 and their most-attended token is the token being written for 59-65% of the copied words. So the heads of the last layer are largely redundant for this model; any specialisation would have to be in the lower layers, which we did not plot.

Table 12. Sharpness of the last decoder layer's cross-attention (mean of heads, averaged over the generated tokens of test articles 0 to 4, recorded during greedy generation).

Run 1 Run 2 (final)
Entropy, as a share of the entropy of a uniform distribution 0.97 0.75
Largest weight, relative to the uniform weight 1.5 x 64 x
Generated word pieces that occur in the article (punctuation excluded) whose most-attended article token is the same piece 6% 64%

The checks in Section 4.2 used five validation articles and the first 60 generated tokens, so their numbers are not directly comparable with this table. The contrast between the two runs is the same.

Is attention an explanation? Partly. The heatmap reliably shows where a copied word comes from: in 64% of the cases the most-attended article token is the word being written. Rows with diffuse attention mark words that the decoder produced from its own context, and these are where invented content such as "for the past month" appears. That makes the heatmap a useful tool for checking a summary against its source. It does not explain why the model chose a span, skipped "john kerry's opposite number" or repeated a sentence. It shows one of the 8 attention layers that feed the output (4 decoder layers with 2 attentions each), averaged over heads, and the output also depends on the decoder's self-attention and feed-forward layers. As the third sentence shows, high attention weights come with false statements as readily as with true ones. This agrees with the caution of Jain and Wallace (2019) that attention weights are not, on their own, an explanation of a model's decision.

7.3 Run 1, for comparison

Figure 8. Run 1, test example 2 (the same article as Figure 6): last-decoder-layer cross-attention (mean of 4 heads) recorded while generating "iranian president ahmadinejad is a former u.s. ambassador to iran ...".

Run 1's heatmap shows what uniform attention looks like. Every weight lies between about 0.0005 and 0.004, around the uniform value of 1/512 = 0.002, and the 60-token window holds 12% of the attention, exactly its share of the 512 tokens. Every row has the same pattern of vertical stripes: punctuation and very common tokens get slightly less attention, other tokens slightly more, whatever word is being generated. The rows for "iranian", "president" and "ambassador" do not single out any article token. The decoder therefore receives roughly the average of the article's representations, which is enough to know the topic but not to copy a name. The generated summary also shows it: the article is about Javad Zarif, the Iranian foreign minister, while the model writes about Ahmadinejad.

8. Discussion

What worked.

  • The from-scratch implementation. The sanity checks passed before training, and the trained model learned behaviour that only a correct encoder-decoder can show: it copies multi-piece names through sharp cross-attention, compresses sentences and ends its summaries properly (only 1 of 11,490 reached the length limit).
  • The preprocessing. The [NL] token taught the model to write separate sentences (3.8 per summary, against 3.9 in the references), which ROUGE-Lsum needs. Truncating articles to 512 tokens keeps about 94% of the reference words that occur in an article, and the model indeed takes most of its content from the start of the article.
  • Diagnosing and fixing the stalled run. This was the decision that mattered most. With the paper's learning rate and batches of 32, the model learned only a topic-conditioned language model (ROUGE-1 13.65). Halving the learning rate and doubling the batch made the cross-attention sharp within the first epoch, and the final model reached ROUGE-1 36.72. Measuring the entropy of the cross-attention was a quick, reliable way to tell the two situations apart long before ROUGE could be computed. One caveat: we changed two settings at once, so we cannot say how much each one contributed.
  • Model selection on the validation set. Every choice used only the validation loss. The test set was used once per run, for the final scores.

What did not work, or only partly.

  • Repetition. 64.8% of the summaries repeat a trigram and 11.7% repeat a whole sentence. Greedy decoding, with no record of what has been said, makes the same continuation likely again after every sentence boundary.
  • Composition errors. The model copies spans correctly but sometimes attaches them to the wrong subject. This was the most frequent factual error in the summaries we read (4 of 9), and the most dangerous one, because the result is fluent and uses only article words.
  • Little abstraction. 22% of the generated sentences are copied word for word and only 39% of the 4-grams are new, against 80% in the references. On this dataset copying is the easiest way to lower the loss, and a 15-million-parameter model trained from scratch has learned that first.
  • Content selection. When the main point is not at the start of the article (opinion pieces such as #184), the model misses it. Most of the gap to Lead-3 comes from content selection, not repetition (Section 5.4).
  • ROUGE does not measure faithfulness. The false sentence in #10377 still earns ROUGE credit, because its words overlap with the reference ("author of ... into the wild", "abc's nightline"). A summary can score close to Lead-3 and still contain false statements, so ROUGE has to be read together with a qualitative check like Section 6.

Limitations of this study. Each run was trained once, with one seed, so we cannot give a variance for the scores (the bootstrap intervals in Table 10 cover only the choice of test articles). Run 2 was stopped by the 20-epoch limit, not by early stopping, so it is not fully converged. The error rates from reading summaries by hand are based on only nine summaries, and the attention analysis covers only the last decoder layer on five articles.

Possible improvements, roughly in order of expected benefit for the effort:

  • Beam search with a length penalty and trigram blocking, to reduce repetition at no training cost.
  • A coverage mechanism (See et al., 2017), which records the attention already given to each article token and penalises attending to it again; it targets the repetition seen in Figure 6 directly.
  • A copy (pointer) mechanism, to get rare names and numbers right.
  • Training longer (the validation loss was still falling) or with a larger model (d_model 512, 6 + 6 layers) if more compute is available.
  • Label smoothing (0.1, as in the paper), which often improves generation quality.
  • Starting from a pre-trained encoder-decoder, which the assignment rules out but which is the standard way to beat Lead-3.

9. Conclusion

We implemented a Transformer encoder-decoder from basic PyTorch layers (multi-head attention, feed-forward network, sinusoidal positional encoding, encoder and decoder layers with the three masks) and trained it on all 287,113 CNN / Daily Mail training pairs. The model has 15.2 million parameters, uses the bert-base-uncased tokenizer with an added sentence token, reads the first 512 tokens of each article and writes up to 128 tokens with greedy decoding.

A first run with the paper's learning-rate schedule stalled. Its cross-attention stayed almost uniform, and it wrote generic text about the right topic (ROUGE-1 13.65). Halving the learning rate and doubling the batch size fixed this. The final model, selected by validation loss (2.324 after 20 epochs), reaches ROUGE-1 36.72, ROUGE-2 15.32, ROUGE-L 25.67 and ROUGE-Lsum 34.33 on the full test set. That is 3.3, 2.2 and 2.0 points below Lead-3 on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-Lsum, 0.65 points above it on ROUGE-L, and roughly the range of the pointer-generator network without coverage.

The attention heatmaps show how the model works. It copies names and phrases through sharp diagonal alignments, shortens sentences by jumping over clauses and occasionally swaps in a synonym. They also show its main weaknesses: it returns to spans it has already copied, which causes repetition, and it can attach a correctly copied span to the wrong subject, which produces fluent but false statements. Beam search with trigram blocking, a coverage mechanism and a copy mechanism are the natural next steps.

Appendix A. How we avoided the assignment's common pitfalls

Pitfall What we did
1. Using nn.Transformer, nn.MultiheadAttention or a pre-trained model All components written from basic layers (Section 3); sanity_checks.py checks that no built-in module is present
2. Missing or wrong causal mask Lower-triangular mask combined with the target padding mask; tested by changing future tokens (Section 3.10)
3. Forgetting the padding mask Source padding mask in encoder self-attention and cross-attention, target padding mask in decoder self-attention; tested by adding padding
4. Counting padding in the loss ignore_index = 0 in training; the validation loss is averaged over non-padding tokens only
5. ROUGE on teacher-forced outputs ROUGE is computed on summaries generated by greedy decoding with no teacher forcing
6. ROUGE-L without saying which Both ROUGE-L and ROUGE-Lsum are reported and labelled
7. Tuning on the test set, or testing the last checkpoint The test set is used only by the final evaluation; early stopping uses the validation set; testing uses the best checkpoint

Appendix C. Reproducing the results

The README.md in the code folder lists the setup and every command. In short:

python sanity_checks.py
python prepare_data.py
python lead3_baseline.py

# run 1: paper's schedule, batch 32; run 2 (final model): half the learning rate, batch 64
python train.py --run_name base
python train.py --run_name lr05_b64 --lr_factor 0.5 --accum 2

# for each run: test-set ROUGE, qualitative examples, attention heatmaps (test articles 0-4)
python evaluate.py --run_dir runs/lr05_b64
python qualitative.py --eval_dir runs/lr05_b64/eval_test
python visualize_attention.py --run_dir runs/lr05_b64 --index 0 --per_head
# Figure 6: all generated rows of test article 2
python visualize_attention.py --run_dir runs/lr05_b64 --index 2 \
    --max_rows 70 --window 70 --per_head

python report/analyze_outputs.py --runs base lr05_b64   # Tables 9-12
python report/make_figures.py --runs base lr05_b64
python report/build_pdf.py
